cls: Oral iron salt (ferrous iron with ascorbic acid)
quick: 100 mg elemental iron daily (per product, e.g. 100 mg ferrous ascorbate)
Best on empty stomach; with food if GI upset; avoid tea/milk/antacids
Used for iron-deficiency anemia in pregnancy as indicated
Use as needed; caution with iron overload risk
Limit; can increase iron absorption/GI irritation
summary: Ferrous ascorbate is an oral iron preparation in which ferrous iron is combined with ascorbic acid (vitamin C) to enhance iron absorption. It is used to treat and prevent iron-deficiency anemia, including in pregnancy. The ascorbate component keeps iron in the better-absorbed ferrous (Fe2+) state and reduces the chelation/oxidation that lowers bioavailability. Common effects are gastrointestinal (constipation, dark stools, nausea); it is not a distinct FDA-approved product but a widely used iron salt, especially in India.
indications: Prophylaxis of iron deficiency, including during pregnancy and in increased-demand states

dosage.d: About 100 mg elemental iron daily (commonly 100 mg ferrous ascorbate, often with folic acid)
dosage.n: Adjust per severity and tolerability; continue 3 months after correction to replenish stores

dosage.d: Per obstetric guidance, commonly 100 mg elemental iron with folic acid daily
dosage.n: Used routinely for antenatal iron supplementation

dosage.d: Approximately 3 mg/kg/day elemental iron in divided doses
dosage.n: Use pediatric formulations; follow product label

admin: Best absorbed on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals; take with food if GI upset occurs
Avoid taking with tea, coffee, milk, eggs, whole grains or antacids, which reduce iron absorption
Separate from calcium supplements, levothyroxine, quinolone/tetracycline antibiotics by at least 2 hours
Do not take with other iron products to avoid overdose
Liquid formulations may stain teeth - dilute and use a straw, rinse afterward
moa: Ferrous iron (Fe2+) is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum and incorporated into hemoglobin, myoglobin and iron-dependent enzymes, correcting iron-deficient erythropoiesis. The ascorbic acid (vitamin C) component acts as a reducing agent that maintains iron in the more readily absorbed ferrous state and prevents its oxidation/chelation, thereby improving the bioavailability of the iron.

absolute: Anemias not due to iron deficiency (e.g. hemolytic, sideroblastic) unless iron deficiency coexists
relative: Active peptic ulcer, regional enteritis, ulcerative colitis (GI irritation)
monitor: Patients on long-term therapy for iron overload
Concurrent drugs whose absorption iron impairs

preg: Iron supplementation, including ferrous ascorbate with folic acid, is routinely used to treat and prevent iron-deficiency anemia in pregnancy and is considered appropriate when indicated.
lact: Iron is compatible with breastfeeding and is used as clinically indicated; only small amounts pass into milk.
renal: Oral iron can be used in renal impairment for iron-deficiency anemia, though intravenous iron is often preferred in advanced CKD; avoid contributing to iron overload and monitor iron indices.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment; use with general caution in significant liver disease.

moderate: Levothyroxine - iron reduces absorption; separate by >= 4 hours
Fluoroquinolone and tetracycline antibiotics - chelation reduces absorption of both; separate by >= 2 hours
Bisphosphonates, methyldopa, levodopa, penicillamine - reduced absorption; separate dosing
Antacids, calcium, proton pump inhibitors/H2 blockers - decrease iron absorption
minor: Ascorbic acid may slightly increase iron absorption (intended effect)
interactions.food: Tea, coffee (tannins), milk/dairy, eggs and whole-grain (phytates) reduce iron absorption; vitamin C-containing foods enhance it.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; chronic intake can increase iron absorption and add GI irritation.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause falsely positive fecal occult blood interpretation in some assays; raises serum iron/ferritin.

serious: Iron overload with inappropriate long-term use
emergency: Acute iron poisoning (especially accidental ingestion by children) - vomiting, GI bleeding, shock, metabolic acidosis, hepatotoxicity

monitoring: Hemoglobin and reticulocyte response (rise expected within 1-2 weeks)
Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation to confirm repletion
Avoid prolonged use without documented iron deficiency
counsel: Take preferably on an empty stomach, but with food if it upsets your stomach; avoid tea, coffee, milk and antacids around the dose
Your stools will turn black - this is normal and harmless
Keep iron tablets away from children - accidental overdose can be life-threatening
Continue for the full course (often a few months) to rebuild iron stores even after blood counts normalize
pk: Reticulocyte rise in 3-7 days; hemoglobin rises over weeks
Iron absorption mainly in duodenum within hours
Iron is recycled, not cleared by a simple half-life
Daily dosing; stores replenish over weeks to months
Store in a cool, dry place, away from children; protect from moisture
pearls: Not a distinct FDA-approved product; record based on standard oral-iron pharmacology and Indian product information, pending clinical review. Widely used in India.
Ascorbic acid keeps iron in the absorbable ferrous state and improves bioavailability vs plain ferrous salts
Separate from levothyroxine, quinolones/tetracyclines and calcium to avoid chelation; avoid tea/coffee around dosing
Iron is a leading cause of fatal accidental poisoning in young children - emphasize safe storage
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one. Do not double up. Continue the daily course for the full recommended duration.
overdose: Acute iron overdose is a medical emergency, especially in children: it causes vomiting, GI bleeding, lethargy, metabolic acidosis, shock and later hepatic failure. Seek emergency care; treatment may include supportive measures, gastric decontamination and chelation with deferoxamine.
